headings.title: Introduction to Nutritional Science and Dietetics
headings.content: Dietetics and nutritional science form the physiological foundation of patient recovery and health promotion. Nutrients are chemical substances obtained from food that provide energy, structural materials, and regulating factors for biochemical processes. The human body requires these elements in precise amounts to sustain cellular metabolism, tissue repair, and immune defense. In clinical practice, understanding how exogenous substances translate into endogenous energy prevents malnutrition-related complications and accelerates convalescence across surgical and medical wards.

headings.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats
headings.content:
Macronutrients are required in large quantities to supply energy and structural integrity. 

- **Carbohydrates**: The body's primary and most rapid source of energy, yielding approximately four kilocalories per gram. They break down into simple sugars like glucose, which fuels the central nervous system and exercising muscle.
- **Proteins**: Composed of amino acids, proteins are indispensable for tissue synthesis, enzyme production, and immune function. Essential amino acids cannot be synthesized internally and must be ingested through the diet.
- **Fats**: Lipids deliver a dense energy source of nine kilocalories per gram, cushion vital organs, facilitate fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and form cellular membrane structures.

headings.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content:
Vitamins and minerals, though required in minute amounts, act as vital co-factors and structural components that regulate physiological equilibrium.

| Micronutrient Type | Primary Subcategories | Core Physiological Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Vitamins** | Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) & Water-soluble (B-complex, C) | Co-enzymes in energy metabolism, vision, and antioxidant defense |
| **Minerals** | Macrominerals (Calcium, Potassium) & Trace elements (Iron, Zinc) | Fluid balance, nerve conduction, and oxygen transport via hemoglobin |

Deficiencies in these regulatory compounds disrupt complex enzymatic reactions, manifesting as distinct clinical syndromes such as scurvy, anemia, or rickets.

headings.title: The Physiological Role of Water
headings.content: Water constitutes over half of total body weight and serves as the universal solvent for all biochemical reactions. It maintains vascular volume, regulates core body temperature through perspiration, lubricates joints, and flushes metabolic waste products via the kidneys. Fluid imbalances rapidly compromise hemodynamic stability, leading to cellular dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, and acute kidney injury if uncorrected.

headings.title: Dietary Fiber and Digestive Health
headings.content:
Dietary fiber consists of plant-derived carbohydrate portions that resist enzymatic digestion in the human small intestine. 

- **Soluble fiber**: Dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance, slowing gastric emptying and helping modulate serum cholesterol and blood glucose levels.
- **Insoluble fiber**: Passes through the digestive tract largely unchanged, adding bulk to stool and stimulating peristalsis to prevent constipation.

Adequate fiber intake maintains a healthy gut microbiome by acting as a prebiotic substrate for beneficial colon bacteria.

headings.title: Nutrient Sources in Local Nigerian Diets
headings.content: Understanding indigenous food patterns is essential for providing culturally competent dietary counseling in Nigeria. Staple foods supply diverse macronutrients and micronutrients tailored to local agricultural outputs. Cassava derivatives like garri and fufu provide dense carbohydrates, while beans, cowpeas, and melon seeds (egusi) offer rich plant-based proteins. Local green leafy vegetables such as fluted pumpkin leaves (ugu) and jute mallow (ewedu) supply vital iron, calcium, and vitamins A and C. Palm oil is a rich, accessible source of beta-carotene and dietary fats.

headings.title: Assessing Nutritional Status and Deficiencies
headings.content: Nutritional assessment involves clinical evaluation, anthropometric measurements, and biochemical testing to identify imbalances. Anthropometric indicators include body mass index, mid-upper arm circumference, and skinfold thickness. Clinical examinations look for physical signs of malnutrition, such as pallor, angular stomatitis, or muscle wasting. Nurses play a frontline role in screening patients upon admission to catch hidden deficiencies before they impair recovery.

headings.title: Promoting Balanced Nutrition in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Clinical application bridges nutritional science and bedside patient care. Nurses translate complex dietary guidelines into practical, culturally appropriate meal plans tailored to individual health conditions. Whether managing diabetic meal timing, low-sodium restrictions for hypertension, or high-protein diets for wound healing, education must match the patient's lifestyle and financial realities. Effective advocacy ensures that nutrition remains an active pillar of holistic nursing care rather than an afterthought.
